summary: Describes the DNS Naming Authority Pointer (NAPTR) record, which carries a regular-expression rewrite rule that turns a string into a new domain label or URI. It was replaced by later documents, RFC 3401 through RFC 3404.

eli5.summary: A phone book entry that says, if you have this kind of name, rewrite it this way to find where to go next. DNS can store such rewrite rules.

questions: how do naptr and srv work together
subtitle: A DNS resource record type that stores regular expression rewrite rules to transform one string into another.

tldr.problem: DNS can look up domain names, but some applications need to transform non-domain strings (like URNs or phone numbers) into domain names or URIs using rewrite rules, and there was no standard way to store these rules.
tldr.mechanism: NAPTR records carry a regular expression substitution rule and an order/preference field. A client applies the regex to a string to produce a new domain name, then looks up NAPTR records at that new domain to continue the chain until reaching a terminal result.
tldr.outcome: NAPTR enabled applications like URN resolution and ENUM (phone number to URI mapping) to be deployed via DNS. However, RFC 2915 was superseded by RFC 3401-3404, which refined the specification.

today: RFC 3401, RFC 3402, RFC 3403, and RFC 3404 obsolete this document. They define ENUM (E.164 Number Mapping) in detail and supersede NAPTR's original specification with refined definitions and clearer semantics.

sections.title: Domain Names from Any String
sections.content:
RFC 2915 defines the Naming Authority Pointer (NAPTR) resource record, which stores a regular expression that transforms one string into another. This allows DNS to be used not just for domain name lookups, but for applications that need to map arbitrary strings (like URNs, email addresses, or phone numbers) into domain names or URIs.

The NAPTR record type (code 35) was originally created by the URN Working Group but has broader utility. A NAPTR record contains order and preference fields to control the sequence of rule application, flags to determine the next lookup type, a service identifier, and a regular expression substitution pattern.
sections.eli5: A NAPTR record is a transformation rule stored in DNS. It says 'when you see this kind of input, rewrite it this way,' so you can start with something that is not a domain name and end up with one.

sections.title: Record Structure and Fields
sections.content:
A NAPTR record contains six main fields:

Order is a 16-bit integer (0-65535) that determines the sequence in which NAPTR records are tried. Lower numbers are processed first, and once a matching record is found, records with higher order values are skipped. Preference (also 0-65535) sorts records with equal order values, similar to MX record preference. Once an order matches, all preference values for that order are candidates; records with different orders are never considered together.

Flags control rewriting behavior. The 'S' flag says the next lookup should be for SRV records. 'A' means look up A/AAAA/A6 address records. 'U' means the result is a URI. 'P' delegates to a protocol-specific algorithm. Service identifies available services and protocols. Regexp contains the POSIX extended regular expression and substitution pattern. Replacement is a fully-qualified domain name used when the regexp is a simple replacement (not a pattern match).
sections.eli5: Order and Preference decide which rule to try first, Flags say what to do with the result, Service says what you can use, and Regexp is the transformation rule itself.

sections.title: Regular Expression Substitution
sections.content:
The Regexp field contains a substitution expression following a defined grammar. The expression consists of a delimiter character (such as '/') followed by a POSIX extended regular expression, another delimiter, a replacement string, another delimiter, and optional flags.

For example, '/urn:cid:.+@([^.]+\.)(.*)$/\2/i' extracts the domain part of a URN-style CID. The replacement uses backreferences (\1, \2, etc.) to refer to capture groups in the regex. The 'i' flag makes matching case-insensitive. Regular expressions are applied only to the original input string, never cumulatively to previous results, to avoid fault-sensitive chains.
sections.eli5: The substitution expression is like a find-and-replace rule. It uses regex wildcards to capture parts of the input and backreferences (\1, \2) to plug them into the output.

sections.title: The NAPTR Resolution Algorithm
sections.content:
The NAPTR algorithm is a looping process: (1) Start with a known domain and a target string. (2) Look up NAPTR records for that domain. (3) Sort by Order, then by Preference. (4) For each record in order, check if it matches: either it has a Replacement field, or its Regexp matches the target string. (5) If a match is found, examine the Flags field. If the flags are terminal (S, A, U, or P), stop and use that result. Otherwise, apply the rewrite rule to produce a new domain and loop back to step 2 with the new domain (but the same target string).

This iterative approach allows complex name transformations to be broken into manageable steps and delegated across different DNS zones. For example, a phone number might first be converted to a domain, then further refined by rules at that domain.
sections.eli5: The algorithm tries one rule after another on your original string. Each successful rule produces a new domain name. Non-terminal rules loop back for more rules at the new domain, until a terminal flag says 'stop here, you are done.'

sections.title: URN and ENUM Applications
sections.content:
NAPTR was designed for URN (Uniform Resource Name) resolution. A URN like 'urn:cid:39CB83F7.A8450130@fake.gatech.edu' can be transformed via NAPTR records at 'cid.urn.arpa' into a domain name like 'gatech.edu'. Further NAPTR records at that domain can then point to SRV records identifying resolver services.

The ENUM application uses NAPTR differently: it converts phone numbers (e.g., '+1-770-555-1212') by removing non-digits, reversing them, adding dots between digits, and appending '.e164.arpa.' NAPTR records at the resulting domain map that phone number to URIs (sip: or mailto:) identifying how to contact that service. This allows phone numbers to be dialed via Internet protocols.
sections.eli5: URN resolution turns an identifier (like a library catalog number) into a domain where a resolver lives. ENUM turns a phone number into the same kind of domain, so anyone can look up how to reach that phone via the Internet.

sections.title: Integration with SRV Records
sections.content:
When a NAPTR record has the 'S' flag, it indicates that the result should be used in an SRV record lookup. SRV records (RFC 2782) specify hosts and ports providing a service at a given domain. However, the domain name produced by NAPTR is used directly in the SRV query without transformation; it is not constructed according to the SRV underscore naming convention (e.g., '_http._tcp.domain'). This subtle difference from typical SRV usage is important for correct implementation.

The Flags field determines the next step: 'S' for SRV, 'A' for address records (which must use default ports since no port is specified in NAPTR), or 'U' for a URI result that requires no further lookup.
sections.eli5: NAPTR produces a domain name, and if the Flags field says 'S', that name goes straight into an SRV lookup to find servers and ports.
